vignette:
Nadia Haddad, a 59-year-old police officer, described the assault as the moment her sense of safety split in two. Months earlier, she had been off duty and riding in a car with a colleague when they stopped near a disturbance. A man turned on her with sudden violence. What stayed with her most was not only the physical threat but the soundscape of it: shouting, the scrape and impact of bodies, her own breath and heartbeat pounding so hard that it seemed to fill her ears. She remembered the scene with painful clarity, down to small visual details and the exact sounds she heard. When the memory came back now, it did not feel like something finished and past; it brought back the same terror she had felt in the moment.

In the weeks that followed, certain experiences began to set everything off. Riding or driving with other people was especially difficult because being in a car with someone else pulled her straight back to the assault. Exposure to violence on the job, even routine police work she had once handled without hesitation, could do the same. Most unsettling of all was her own body: if her heart started racing, she did not experience it as a passing stress response but as a warning that danger was already here. Once she noticed that pounding in her chest, she became convinced her body was reacting as if she were still under attack. Those moments also strengthened her belief that she could not rely on other people to keep her safe, and that what had happened to her was profoundly unjust and unresolved.

Because she had come to believe her body could turn against her without warning, Nadia started watching herself closely. She monitored her thoughts for any sign that she was losing her mind, scanning internally whenever she felt activated. She also watched other people with the same intensity, studying faces, postures, and movements for evidence of threat. Over time she withdrew more and more, cutting off friends and extended family rather than risk being around people she no longer trusted. The unfairness of the assault remained fixed in her mind, and the sense that nothing meaningful had been done about it hardened her distance from others; if people and systems had failed her once, she saw little reason to lean on them now.

The memories did not soften with time. They remained vivid and sharply detailed, and when they came, she sometimes heard in her head the same sounds from the assault. That auditory quality was particularly destabilizing. Hearing those sounds internally made the memory feel as if it were happening again, and the terror surged up with it. After these episodes she would isolate further, avoiding calls and family gatherings, and becoming even more determined to keep constant watch over both her surroundings and her own mind. The more the memory arrived in this raw, sensory form, the more certain she felt that her body was unsafe and that she was essentially on her own.

Her efforts to manage this left her life increasingly constricted. At work, being a police officer meant she could not avoid all contact with violence, but she tried to control what she could. If she had to ride with someone, she stayed braced and alert, already listening for changes in her breathing and heartbeat. If her chest began to pound, her attention snapped inward and outward at once: inward to check whether she was “going crazy,” outward to search for dangerous people. That constant monitoring seemed to prime the next episode. The more she scanned for signs of danger in her body and in others, the more quickly she noticed her heart racing; the more she noticed it, the more easily the memory broke through, complete with sound and terror. Each recurrence seemed to confirm for her that her body could not be trusted and that other people were unreliable.

At home, her husband saw how much smaller her world had become. Nadia no longer reached out to friends or relatives, and she kept conversations short because any emotional arousal could make her aware of her heartbeat. The isolation left her alone with the memory, and in that silence the assault returned with even greater force. She said that when the sounds came back in her head, she felt again the same certainty that she was in immediate danger. By the time she sought help, what frightened her most was not just remembering the assault but the feeling that her own body, other people, and the world around her had all become untrustworthy. What she hoped for, cautiously, was to be able to sit in a car with someone, do her job, and hear her heart race without believing she was back there again.
